items.title: 52060_Eddie Barefield oral history interview
items.q: When did you go to Europe with Sammy Price? [INTERVIEWEE] 1958.

ctx.x: And I wrote in double what the other guys were getting. But anyway, now, I made about three, $4,000.00 for the music that I had written, you know, but this was one quirk of life, things, the way things happen.

items.title: 67460_Sammy Price oral history interview
items.q: Eddie Barefield always said that every town that I went in over the years, Sam Price was always sure with a woman.

ctx.x: some money you'd say, 'Now, when you get down in Shreveport, give this to my aunt and stay with her that week.' And maybe coming from the other way, Louisville, you come back down to Winston-Salem and back down and all until you get to Shreveport and you give the money to the parent or the mother of the friend, and so forth. So, I think that, that one thing that that thing taught you was fidelity, friendship and respect and recognition. Now we don't practice that all the time, that's an important fact. For…

have been like that with musicians, that I would share what I have, like I knew how to...well, I won't say I knew how to get money from women, but I knew...well, you know, women liked me and they would want to do me favors, and if some guy...you understand, Dan, wasn't doing too well, he could always come to me. That guy was here, right here. One time I owed my rent...my rent was a thousand dollars and his rent was a hundred and I had a hundred dollars. And you know what I did? I gave it to him. He paid his rent.…

You know, Danny, during those years singers were the principals. You don't think that Coleman Hawkins could take his tenor saxophone player and go out and stand in front of Butter-Beans and Susie and be the star. He was just another musician in the background.
